promise: After this you can explain what a CDN is, how a request is answered at the edge, and what a CDN is allowed to cache.

terms.definition: How long a packet takes to go to a server and back; distance adds to it.
The server that holds the real content, which a CDN sits in front of.
A location close to users, far from the origin, where copies of content are kept.

before.note: Read DNS and Caching first: a CDN uses DNS to send you to a nearby edge and caches content there. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: Distance costs time. A user in one country fetching from a server in another pays for every round trip across the network. web.dev explains a content delivery network, a CDN, as servers placed closer to users than the origin, so a request has a shorter round trip, with caches that can answer without contacting the origin at all [[webdev-cdn]].

At its heart a CDN is a cache, the topic you just read, placed away from your application and near users. MDN counts CDNs as managed caches, ones a service developer sets up on purpose to take load off the origin, and says that in most cases you control them with the Cache-Control header and your own configuration [[mdn-caching]]. The same ideas apply: a hit is served locally and fast, a miss fetches from the origin, and web.dev says a CDN's cache is built up over time as additional uncached resources are requested [[webdev-cdn]].

The result is lower latency for users and less load on the origin. web.dev says that because CDNs reduce server load they reduce server costs and are well suited to handling traffic spikes [[webdev-cdn]].

terms.definition: A worldwide network of servers that cache and serve content close to users.
A CDN server near users that answers requests from a cached copy.
A CDN location, usually in a specific city or region, holding edge servers.
The authoritative server the CDN pulls from on a miss.
The share of traffic the CDN serves so the origin never sees it.

stages.name: How it works
body: The first job is getting each user to the CDN. web.dev's setup steps are to sign up with a CDN provider and update your CNAME DNS record to point at it; as a result of that DNS change, traffic to your site is routed through the CDN [[webdev-cdn]]. This is the direct link to the DNS topic you already read. How a CDN then picks an edge close to the user is not described on that page; many CDNs use the DNS answer or anycast addressing for it.

Once at the edge, the request is a cache lookup. On a hit the edge returns its stored copy. On a miss it fetches from the origin, stores the result, and serves it, so the next nearby user gets a hit. You steer how long the edge keeps a copy through HTTP caching headers such as Cache-Control [[mdn-caching]].

Those headers are the standard contract between the origin and every cache in the path, including the CDN. Cache-Control with max-age sets how long a response stays fresh, and directives like public, private and no-store say whether a shared cache such as a CDN may store it at all [[rfc9111]].

Content splits into kinds that cache differently. web.dev says whether a resource should be cached depends on whether it is public or private, and static or dynamic. Private resources, which contain data for a single user, should not be cached by a CDN, while public resources can be, for a length of time that depends on how often the asset changes. It also says dynamic content that changes frequently can still be cached for very short periods, for example during heavy traffic [[webdev-cdn]].

terms.definition: Many edges sharing one address, with routing sending each user to the nearest.
The share of edge requests served without going to the origin.
The Cache-Control value saying how many seconds a response stays fresh at a cache.
Static content rarely changes and caches well; dynamic, per-user content does not.
A cache serving many users, such as a CDN; only responses marked public belong in it.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: The invalidation problem from caching gets harder across a worldwide network. When content changes, every cache that holds an old copy is stale. web.dev describes purging, also called cache invalidation, as removing a resource from a CDN's caches without waiting for it to expire or be evicted, typically through an API [[webdev-cdn]]. MDN adds that with a CDN that supports purging you can use a more aggressive caching strategy, storing the main resource and purging it only when the server updates it [[mdn-caching]].

A common pattern avoids purging altogether. MDN calls it cache busting: resources that work best with caching are static immutable files, and for resources that change it is a common best practice to change the URL each time the content changes, using a version number or hash value in the name, so the URL can be cached for a longer period [[mdn-caching]]. That is why build tools put a hash in asset filenames.

Validators let a cache refresh cheaply. MDN describes validation as a way to turn a stale response into a fresh one by asking the origin, using a conditional request with If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match, where an ETag is a value generated by the server such as a hash of the body [[mdn-caching]]. The standard rules for validation are in RFC 9111 section 4.3 [[rfc9111]].

terms.definition: Actively removing a cached copy from edges before it would expire.
Changing a file's URL, often with a content hash, so a new version is fetched fresh.
A tag identifying a version of a response, used to check if a cached copy is still current.
Asking the origin whether a stale copy is still good, getting a small reply if it is.
A short reply saying the cached copy is still valid, avoiding a full transfer.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The central trade-off is freshness against reach, and web.dev adds a second one: a CDN's performance strategy is a tradeoff between minimising latency and maximising cache hit ratio, because a CDN with many points of presence can deliver lower latency but may see lower hit ratios as traffic is split across more caches [[webdev-cdn]]. A long max-age gives a high hit ratio, but a change takes longer to appear unless you purge; a short one keeps content fresh but sends more traffic back to the origin.

A CDN changes failure and cost too. With most traffic absorbed at the edge, the origin can be smaller and a traffic spike is less dangerous. But a misconfigured cache can serve personal data to the wrong user: MDN warns that it would be problematic if a personalised response is visible to other users of a cache, and says the private directive keeps it stored only with that client [[mdn-caching]].

A CDN only helps what it can cache. web.dev's conclusion is to cache content as aggressively as possible, static and dynamic, for varying durations, and to audit your site periodically to make sure you are caching optimally [[webdev-cdn]]. This is the same lesson as plain caching, now measured across the whole network: know what fraction of requests can be served from a copy.

terms.definition: The share of requests the CDN serves from the edge; higher means more offload.
A layer that funnels edge misses through one point so the origin sees fewer duplicate fetches.
public lets a shared cache store a response; private forbids it, for per-user data.
How much of your traffic can be served from a cached copy; it bounds the CDN's benefit.

misconceptions.myth: A CDN is something different from a cache.
misconceptions.truth: MDN lists CDNs among managed caches, and web.dev describes CDN caches that answer requests without going to the origin [[mdn-caching]] [[webdev-cdn]].
It helps what it can cache. web.dev says private resources, which contain data for one user, should not be cached by a CDN [[webdev-cdn]].

misconceptions.myth: Changing content updates every edge instantly.
misconceptions.truth: A cache can keep a stored response until it expires or is purged, so web.dev describes purging as the way to remove a resource without waiting for it to expire [[webdev-cdn]].

misconceptions.myth: It is safe to cache any response at the edge.
misconceptions.truth: MDN says a personalised response visible to other users of a cache is a problem, and that the private directive prevents it [[mdn-caching]].

tryIt.intro: This uses curl, the command-line tool, to look at the response headers a site sends. The command is the one in the curl manual; replace the address with a site you know is served through a CDN to see headers such as Cache-Control and Age, which MDN describes. The address https://example.com is the manual's own example. Output depends on the site, so it is not shown here.

commands.shows: Fetches the headers only, using an HTTP HEAD request, as the manual describes for -I. Look for Cache-Control and Age.

next: Go back to the CDNs topic page for the worked example and the quiz, then read the two company posts on running a CDN. The caching trade-offs here recur in Replication and Sharding, where copies and splits are managed closer to the data.
